content.text: Several agents beat one when the work splits into independent parts that each need their own searching and context. Anthropic's research system, built that way, beat a single agent by 90.2% on its internal eval, but multi-agent systems used about 15 times the tokens of a chat, and a study of seven open-source frameworks found them failing on 41% to 86.7% of tasks. Add agents for breadth you can verify, not by default.

A team asks their new multi-agent research system a simple question: which of their twelve competitors include SSO in the cheapest plan? The lead agent spawns dozens of subagents. Several research the same vendor, two come back with marketing pages and no prices, and the lead merges pages of raw notes into a confident table with three wrong rows. The run costs many times what their old single agent spent on the same question, and nobody can say which subagent got which row wrong.
The common misconception
"Splitting a task across several cooperating agents always gives better results than a single agent." It sounds right:

items.text: The headline results are real: Anthropic's multi-agent research system beat a single agent by 90.2% on its internal evaluation.
It mirrors human teams: specialists, division of labor, a manager who delegates.
Frameworks make it easy to define a "team" of role-playing agents in a few lines.
Each agent gets a clean context, and the previous article showed why a smaller context helps.

content.text: The half-truth: more agents do win, on a particular kind of task and at a particular price. Outside that, they add cost, latency and new ways to fail.
What actually happens
Where the gain comes from

Anthropic's system uses an orchestrator-worker design: a lead agent plans the research and starts subagents that search in parallel, each in its own context window, and return condensed findings. With Claude Opus 4 as the lead and Claude Sonnet 4 subagents, it beat a single Claude Opus 4 agent by 90.2% on their internal research eval. The gains were largest on breadth-first queries, such as finding the board members of every IT company in the S&P 500, where the single agent searched slowly, one step after another, and failed.

Their explanation is less magical than "teamwork". In their analysis of the BrowseComp benchmark, three factors explained 95% of the performance variance, and token usage alone explained 80%; the number of tool calls and the model choice were the other two. A
multi-agent system

works mainly because it spends enough tokens on the problem, spread across separate context windows. That's the sub-agent pattern from the context engineering article: each worker may use tens of thousands of tokens and hand back a summary of often 1,000 to 2,000.
What it costs

In Anthropic's data, agents used about 4 times the tokens of a chat, and multi-agent systems about 15 times. The task has to be valuable enough to pay for that. They also name poor fits: tasks where all agents need the same context or depend heavily on each other. Most coding tasks have fewer truly parallel parts than research, and as of their 2025 write-up, agents weren't yet good at coordinating and delegating to each other in real time. Even their lead waited for each batch of subagents to finish, so one slow search could block the whole run.
How multi-agent systems fail

Cemri and colleagues analyzed more than 1,600 traces from seven popular open-source multi-agent frameworks, published at NeurIPS 2025. Failure rates ranged from 41% to 86.7%, and they grouped 14 failure modes into three categories:

items.text: agents ignoring the task or their role, repeating steps, or not knowing when the task is done.
drifting off the task, withholding information another agent needed, ignoring other agents' input, or acting against their own stated reasoning.
stopping too early or checking superficially. A ChatDev chess program passed review because it compiled, yet broke the rules of chess.

content.text: Their fixes were design changes, not more agents. Clearer role specifications raised ChatDev's success rate by 9.4% with the same model, GPT-4o, and adding a step that verified the high-level objective raised it by 15.6%. Anthropic hit similar problems early on: agents spawning 50 subagents for simple queries, searching endlessly for sources that didn't exist, and duplicating each other's work when the lead's instructions were vague.
Making it pay off

Anthropic's lessons are concrete. Each subagent needs an objective, an output format, guidance on tools and sources, and clear task boundaries. Effort should scale with the query: one agent with 3 to 10 tool calls for simple fact-finding, 2 to 4 subagents for direct comparisons, more than 10 only for complex research. Running 3 to 5 subagents at once, each calling tools in parallel, cut research time by up to 90% for complex queries.
Here's the competitor question both ways. The split is known, one subtask per vendor, so code does the fan-out. When the split depends on what's found, an
orchestrator
agent plans it, with the same kind of brief and caps.

tabs.label: ❌ Wrong
tabs.code:
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor

question = "Which of our competitors offer SSO on the cheapest plan?"
topics = plan_subtasks(question)  # the lead decides; often far too many
with ThreadPoolExecutor() as pool:  # no cap on parallel subagents
    results = list(pool.map(lambda t: run_agent(f"Research {t}"), topics))
print(write_report(question, "\n".join(results)))  # raw dumps, no checks

tabs.label: ✅ Right
tabs.code:
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor

question = "Which of our competitors offer SSO on the cheapest plan?"
BRIEF = ("Objective: does {v}'s cheapest plan include SSO? "
         "Use only {v}'s own pricing and docs pages. "
         "Return one line: '<yes|no|unclear> | <plan> | <source URL>'.")


def check(vendor):  # one independent subtask with a clear boundary
    return run_agent(BRIEF.format(v=vendor))


with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=4) as pool:  # cap parallel agents
    rows = dict(zip(COMPETITORS, pool.map(check, COMPETITORS)))
unclear = [v for v, row in rows.items() if not row.startswith(("yes", "no"))]
if unclear:  # checked in code before anything is reported
    print("Needs a human look:", unclear)
print(write_report(question, rows))  # the lead reads short rows, not pages

content.text: Each subagent now has one vendor, one kind of source and a one-line format, and the lead reads short rows instead of pages of notes. A row that isn't a clear yes or no goes to a person instead of into the report.

rows.text: Coupled tasks that need shared context, like most coding
Broad tasks that split into independent searches
Each worker has its own; the lead sees summaries
Duplicated work, lost information, shallow verification

content.text: Anthropic recommends letting subagents store their work in external systems, such as files, and hand the lead a lightweight reference. That avoids a game of telephone through the coordinator and the token cost of copying large outputs through the conversation.

In the traces Cemri and colleagues studied, many verifier agents only checked whether code compiled or had leftover TODO comments, even when prompted to verify thoroughly. Put the checks you trust in code, such as tests, schemas and source lookups, and evaluate the end state, not the conversation.
How to apply it in your project
Build the single-agent version first, with good tools and context, and measure it on your eval.

items.title: Check the shape of the task

content.text: Go multi-agent only if the work splits into independent parts, each needs real searching or context, and the result is worth many times the tokens.
Give each subagent an objective, an output format, the tools and sources to use, and what's out of scope.
Scale the number of subagents to the task, and cap concurrency, tool calls and spend per run.
Check outputs in code, then compare success rate, tokens and latency with the single-agent baseline on the same eval.
Key takeaways

items.text: Multi-agent systems win mainly by spending more tokens in separate, parallel contexts; in Anthropic's analysis, token usage alone explained 80% of BrowseComp performance variance.
That costs about 15 times the tokens of a chat, so the task has to be worth it.
They fit broad, parallel work; tightly coupled tasks, like most coding, usually don't.
They bring new failures, such as vague delegation, lost information and shallow verification: failure rates of 41% to 86.7% across seven open-source frameworks.
Start with one agent, and add subagents with clear briefs, caps and code-level checks only where an eval shows a gain.
